body:
@Namey5 The changes to the shader did the trick for now. Thank you very much for the suggestion!

Over the past few days, I tried to find other scenarios where switching the render engine could cause a discrepancy in the shader behavior due to the different handling of `VERTEX`. So far I could not find any; I was especially worried about "Signed Distance Fields/Functions", but all the ones I tried behaved as expected.

# Suggestion
Even if a implementation of  `glProvokingVertex` would be done at some point, it would be helpful (in the mean time and also later, if other, similar discrepancies should occur) to have a column for remarks regarding the render engine compatibility in the [documentation](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/shaders/shader_reference/shading_language.html#interpolation-qualifiers):

## Example:
![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/44c9a312-41f1-4a03-99c6-0c9e3e4add9d)

# Alternative
Alternatively, but less ideal, one could add a general section about all the known differences between the render engines to the [Shading Language Reference](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/shaders/shader_reference/shading_language.html).

While the convention could be set to match Vulkan, it doesn't solve the issue.
`glProvokingVertex(GL_FIRST_VERTEX_CONVENTION)` just change the issue from y to x.

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/81a4393b-fd6f-4686-a925-ffcc7c54fc26)

> While the conversion could be set to match Vulkan, it doesn't solve the issue. `glProvokingVertex(GL_FIRST_VERTEX_CONVENTION)` just change the issue from y to x.

Hmm, this makes me wonder if triangle indices are also pushed in a different order in the backends. Time for some more investigation, I suppose!
